block.semiconductor-lab.refrigerator.not: A machine that runs on electricity and freezes water. A relative of refrigerators and air conditioners.
Compressor + 2 copper + 6 iron. 1 kW, 20 s. One ammonia water in the refrigerant slot (not used up); water bucket -> ice (the bucket returns).

In 1876 the German Linde built an ammonia compression refrigerating machine, letting breweries cool without winter ice. Linde later liquefied air to separate oxygen and nitrogen ([6-07] air separation).

The compressed, heated refrigerant is cooled outside into a liquid, then expanded suddenly through a narrow opening so it evaporates and draws heat from around it. It moves heat from cold to hot, so it is also called a heat pump. Semiconductor fab air conditioning and constant temperature ([12-12], [8-07]) work the same way.
block.semiconductor-lab.refrigerator.pla: Approximation: the real refrigerant is anhydrous ammonia (ammonia water here). Vanilla has no food spoilage, so there is no refrigerator function.
item.semiconductor-lab.vinegar.note1: A sour liquid you get by leaving alcohol open to the air.
item.semiconductor-lab.vinegar.note2: Put fermented wash (alcohol) in a fermentation crock and wait for 2. 2 vinegar + sodium hydroxide -> sodium acetate. About 5% acetic acid.
item.semiconductor-lab.vinegar.note3: Acetic acid bacteria from the air turn alcohol into acetic acid with oxygen: C2H5OH + O2 -> CH3COOH + H2O.
item.semiconductor-lab.vinegar.note4: In 1864 Pasteur showed that vinegar is made by acetic acid bacteria (Mycoderma aceti). Vinegar is humanity's first acid, thousands of years older than acetic acid from wood vinegar [2-23].
item.semiconductor-lab.vinegar.placehold: Approximation: acetic acid strength is fixed.
Alcohol warmed a little to cut down the germs in it. It will not turn to vinegar in the crock.
Warm fermented wash briefly on a campfire. The fermentation crock refuses it (no germs, so no vinegar). Compare with unheated wash.
A few minutes at about 60 C reduces the souring and spoiling germs without changing the taste. Boiling would drive off the alcohol and change the flavour.
In 1864 Pasteur showed this prevents the 'disease' that soured French wine. 'Pasteurize' on milk cartons is his name.
Approximation: the temperature is represented by a campfire.
item.semiconductor-lab.cane_juice.note1: Sweet juice pressed from sugar cane, cleared with lime.
item.semiconductor-lab.cane_juice.note2: 3 sugar cane + slaked lime + water bucket (bucket returned). Boil down on a campfire for 2 raw sugar.
item.semiconductor-lab.cane_juice.note3: Lime neutralizes the juice's acids and makes proteins and other cloudiness clump and settle (clarification).
item.semiconductor-lab.cane_juice.note4: Cane sugar has been made in India since around the start of the common era. Sanskrit 'sharkara' (grains of sand) is where 'sugar' comes from.
item.semiconductor-lab.cane_juice.placeh: Approximation: pressing and straining are skipped.
item.semiconductor-lab.beet_juice.note1: Sweet juice soaked out of sugar beet roots.
item.semiconductor-lab.beet_juice.note2: 4 beetroot + slaked lime + water bucket (bucket returned). Boil down on a campfire for 2 raw sugar.
item.semiconductor-lab.beet_juice.note3: Beet sugar is exactly the same sucrose, C12H22O11, as cane sugar.
item.semiconductor-lab.beet_juice.note4: Marggraf in Germany found sugar in beets in 1747, and Achard built the first beet sugar factory in 1801, so cold countries without cane could make sugar (it spread under Napoleon's Continental Blockade).
item.semiconductor-lab.beet_juice.placeh: Approximation: vanilla beetroot stands in for sugar beet (real sugar beet has a white root).
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_sugar.note1: Brown sugar from boiling down the juice. It still holds much colour and flavour.
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_sugar.note2: Boil juice down on a campfire for 2. 2 raw sugar + bone char + water bucket -> 2 white sugar.
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_sugar.note3: As the water boils off and it thickens, sucrose crystallizes. The surrounding molasses (brown liquid) carries the colour.
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_sugar.note4: Okinawan kokuto is cane juice simply boiled down like this.
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_sugar.placeho: Approximation: centrifuging off the molasses is skipped.
item.semiconductor-lab.bone_char.note1: Black grains from charred bone. They soak up colour very well.
item.semiconductor-lab.bone_char.note2: Char bones in a furnace (an approximation of heating without air). Used to turn raw sugar white (used up).
item.semiconductor-lab.bone_char.note3: Carbon coats the tiny pores of the bone's calcium phosphate, trapping the large colour molecules in them (adsorption).
item.semiconductor-lab.bone_char.note4: Used to decolourize sugar since the 19th century; activated carbon and ion exchange resins [2-17] are also used today.
item.semiconductor-lab.bone_char.placeho: Approximation: re-burning it for reuse is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_can.note1: An iron can with a thin coat of tin. It hardly rusts.
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_can.note2: Iron + tin -> 4. Add cooked meat or fish to make a sealed can.
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_can.note3: Tinplate is iron sheet dipped in molten tin. In 1810 Peter Durand in England patented keeping food in tin cans.
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_can.note4: For about 50 years after canning was invented there were no can openers; soldiers used bayonets or chisels ⚠️.
item.semiconductor-lab.sealed_can.note1: A filled, closed can. Not heated yet, so not canned food yet.
item.semiconductor-lab.sealed_can.note2: Heat it in a furnace or campfire to make canned food.
item.semiconductor-lab.sealed_can.note3: The key is to close it before heating: heat kills the germs inside, and the seal keeps new ones out. Heating first and closing afterwards lets germs in.
item.semiconductor-lab.sealed_can.note4: Appert did not know why it worked. The reason (germs) became clear about 50 years later through Pasteur's work in the 1860s.
item.semiconductor-lab.sealed_can.placeh: Approximation: real cans are boiled a long time in water (today at 120 °C under pressure). In the game you heat it in a furnace or campfire.
item.semiconductor-lab.canned_meat.note1: Food you can carry a long time. A little more filling than cooked meat.
item.semiconductor-lab.canned_meat.note2: Heat a sealed can in a furnace or campfire. Hunger 9 (cooked beef is 8).
item.semiconductor-lab.canned_meat.note3: In 1804-10, Nicolas Appert in France found that food packed into bottles, sealed and boiled kept for a long time, winning Napoleon's army prize. Tin cans came after.
item.semiconductor-lab.canned_meat.note4: Heating kills the germs, the seal keeps new ones out. Modern cans last for years.
item.semiconductor-lab.canned_meat.place: Approximation: the extra hunger is a game rule (real nutrition is about the same as cooked meat). No empty can is left. The game has no food spoilage.
A blue spray that protects crops like grapes from mould diseases.
Copper sulfate + slaked lime + water -> 4 (bucket returned). For now it is only crafted; there is no crop disease yet. ⚠ GHS: copper compounds harm aquatic life.

In 1885 Pierre-Marie-Alexis Millardet in France reported that it prevents downy mildew of grapes (a mould). Copper ions stop the spores from sprouting; the lime makes the copper stick to the leaves against rain and spares the leaves.
Bordeaux farmers painted the roadside vines with a blue mixture so passers-by would not steal the grapes - and only those vines escaped the disease. That was the clue.
Approximation: craft only. Crop disease and spraying to prevent it are not in the game (decision Q3-14 ②).
item.semiconductor-lab.superphosphate.no: A phosphorus fertilizer made from bones. Spread on a field, it gives bigger harvests.

3 bone meal + 2 sulfuric acid (bottles returned) -> 3. Use on farmland to make 'fertile farmland' (3 shares of phosphorus): each ripe crop harvested gives 1 extra. Nitrogen fertilizers (peas, ammonium sulfate/nitrate) speed growth; phosphorus adds yield. Spread both and both work.

The calcium phosphate in bone, Ca3(PO4)2, does not dissolve in water, so plants can hardly take it up. Sulfuric acid turns it into water-soluble calcium dihydrogen phosphate Ca(H2PO4)2 (plus gypsum CaSO4). Ca3(PO4)2 + 2H2SO4 -> Ca(H2PO4)2 + 2CaSO4.

John Bennet Lawes patented it in England in 1842 and built the world's first chemical fertilizer factory. His Rothamsted farm has compared fertilizers on the same fields for over 150 years - the oldest agricultural experiment in the world.
item.semiconductor-lab.superphosphate.pl: Approximation: phosphorus is counted as '3 harvests' and works as '1 extra item per harvest'. Bone meal instead of phosphate rock (the real thing also started with bones).
A nitrogen fertilizer. Spread on a field, crops grow faster.
Ammonia + nitric acid (bag and bottle returned). On farmland it gives 3 shares of nitrogen (like ammonium sulfate or peas). ⚠ GHS: oxidizing solid. Keep away from things that burn.
NH3 + HNO3 -> NH4NO3. About 34% of its weight is nitrogen (ammonium sulfate: about 21%), so it carries more nitrogen per kilogram. Half is ammonium and half nitrate, both quickly taken up by plants.

Failure record: large stores of ammonium nitrate have exploded again and again (Oppau, Germany 1921; Texas City, USA 1947; Beirut, Lebanon 2020). Storage rules are strict today. Nitrogen from the air becomes bread - and, mishandled, a disaster.
Approximation: in the game it works the same as ammonium sulfate (the higher nitrogen content is explained only).
item.semiconductor-lab.salted_meat.note1: Meat or fish rubbed with salt. Made without fire, and it keeps a long time.
item.semiconductor-lab.salted_meat.note2: 2 raw meat or fish + salt -> 2. Edible as is (hunger 5). Smoke it in a smoker or campfire for smoked meat.
item.semiconductor-lab.salted_meat.note3: Salt draws water out of the meat (osmosis). Bacteria cannot multiply without water, so it spoils slowly.
item.semiconductor-lab.salted_meat.note4: Salt was once so precious it was called 'white gold'. The word 'salary' is said to come from salt (Latin sal) paid to Roman soldiers ⚠️ (not certain).
item.semiconductor-lab.salted_meat.place: Approximation: the amount of salt and the days of curing are left out. The game has no spoilage.
item.semiconductor-lab.smoked_meat.note1: Salted meat or fish cured in smoke. It keeps a very long time.
item.semiconductor-lab.smoked_meat.note2: Smoke salted meat in a smoker or campfire. Hunger 9 (cooked beef is 8). Chicken or fish fill you just as much.
item.semiconductor-lab.smoked_meat.note3: Phenols and other compounds in smoke kill germs and slow the fat from going rancid. The surface also dries, so it spoils even more slowly.
item.semiconductor-lab.smoked_meat.note4: Until refrigerators ([11-13]) and canning ([11-12]), salted, dried and smoked food fed long sea voyages and winters.
item.semiconductor-lab.smoked_meat.place: Approximation: the extra hunger is a game rule (with water dried out, there is more nutrition per weight).
item.semiconductor-lab.quern.note1: Two stones that grind grain into flour.
item.semiconductor-lab.quern.note2: 3 smooth stone + stick. Use with 2 wheat in a crafting table -> 2 flour (the quern is returned).
item.semiconductor-lab.quern.note3: Turning the upper stone on the lower one crushes the grain between them. Earlier people pushed a hand stone back and forth over a flat stone (saddle quern).
item.semiconductor-lab.quern.note4: Grinding was one of the first jobs people gave to water wheels and windmills. In 1785 Oliver Evans in America built a mill that ran by itself from unloading the grain onwards.
item.semiconductor-lab.quern.placeholder: Approximation: the quern does not wear out (real ones did, and stone grit in the flour wore down people's teeth).
item.semiconductor-lab.flour.note1: Ground grain. The stuff of bread.
item.semiconductor-lab.flour.note2: Quern + 2 wheat -> 2. 3 flour + wild yeast + water -> 2 bread dough.
item.semiconductor-lab.flour.note3: Starch and protein (gluten-forming) from the grain. Kneaded with water, gluten forms a mesh that traps the yeast's carbon dioxide, so the dough rises.
item.semiconductor-lab.flour.note4: In the 1870s, roller milling with iron rollers spread from Hungary, grinding step by step and making white flour cheap.
item.semiconductor-lab.flour.placeholder: Approximation: vanilla bread is made straight from wheat (milling left out). This mod's bread starts from flour.
item.semiconductor-lab.bread_dough.note1: Flour, water and yeast kneaded together. Bake it into risen bread.
item.semiconductor-lab.bread_dough.note2: 3 flour + wild yeast + water (bucket returned) -> 2. Bake in a furnace, smoker or campfire.
item.semiconductor-lab.bread_dough.note3: Yeast eats the sugars in flour and gives off carbon dioxide and alcohol (fermentation [2-39]). The gas bubbles are caught in the gluten mesh and the dough rises.
item.semiconductor-lab.bread_dough.note4: The holes in bread are where the yeast's carbon dioxide bubbles were. Baking drives off the alcohol.
item.semiconductor-lab.bread_dough.place: Approximation: the hours of rising are left out.
item.semiconductor-lab.leavened_bread.no: Bread risen with yeast. More filling than vanilla bread.
Bake bread dough. Hunger 7 (vanilla bread is 5).
Risen bread is easier to digest and bigger from the same flour. Leavened bread is said to have been baked in Egypt around 4000 BC ⚠️.
Why bread rises (the work of a living thing, yeast) became clear only with Pasteur's research in 1857. For thousands of years people baked it without knowing why.
item.semiconductor-lab.leavened_bread.pl: Approximation: the extra hunger is a game rule (compare with vanilla bread as flat, unrisen bread).
message.semiconductor-lab.compost.fertil: Compost (bone meal) spread: a little nitrogen and phosphorus (1 share each)
block.semiconductor-lab.tired_farmland.n: A field that keeps growing the same crop. Too many times in a row and the harvest shrinks.

Harvesting a ripe crop on ordinary farmland makes it remember which crop and how many times in a row. After 3 of the same crop (wheat, einkorn, carrots, potatoes, beetroot), each harvest gives 1 less. To recover: grow a different crop, grow peas, spread compost or fertilizer, or leave it empty for a while (fallow).

The same crop keeps using the same nutrients, and its pests and diseases build up in the soil (continuous-cropping injury). Medieval Europe's three-field system rotated winter crop, spring crop and fallow; livestock grazed the fallow and manured it.

The Norfolk four-course rotation, spread by Charles Townshend in the 1730s, cycled wheat, turnips, barley and clover and did away with fallow. Turnips fed livestock in winter; clover, a legume, added nitrogen. With more animals kept through winter, there was more manure too.
block.semiconductor-lab.tired_farmland.p: Approximation: wear is counted as '3 of the same crop -> harvest -1' (decision Q3-15 ①). There are no turnips or clover (explained only).
item.semiconductor-lab.plow.note1: A farm tool that cuts and turns the soil. Tills a wide area at once.
item.semiconductor-lab.plow.note2: 2 iron + 3 planks + 2 sticks (durability 250). Used on dirt or grass, it turns the 3x3 around into farmland (a hoe does one block).
item.semiconductor-lab.plow.note3: The pointed share cuts the soil and the curved mouldboard turns it over, burying weeds and letting in air. Pulled by oxen or horses, it prepares far more land than people with hoes.
item.semiconductor-lab.plow.note4: Around 4000 BC, wooden scratch ploughs (ards) were used in Mesopotamia. In 1837 John Deere in America made a steel plough that sticky prairie soil would not cling to, and the North American prairies became farmland.
item.semiconductor-lab.plow.placeholder: Approximation: no oxen or horses (the player uses it).
block.semiconductor-lab.salty_farmland.n: A field in dry land that has been watered for years. Salt has built up and harvests shrink.

In desert, savanna and badlands, each harvest from watered (moist) farmland leaves salt behind. After 3, each harvest gives 1 less. Right-click with gypsum (calcium sulfate) to turn it back into farmland.

River and ground water carry a little dissolved salt. In dry land the water evaporates and the salt stays in the soil; with too much salt, roots cannot take up water. Calcium from gypsum swaps for sodium in the soil so it washes out more easily.

In Sumer in Mesopotamia, salt built up in long-irrigated fields, and crops are said to have shifted from salt-sensitive wheat to salt-tolerant barley ⚠️. Many irrigated fields worldwide still suffer from salinity today.
block.semiconductor-lab.salty_farmland.p: Approximation: salt is counted as '3 irrigated harvests in dry land -> -1'. Drainage and rising ground water are omitted.
message.semiconductor-lab.salty_farmland: Gypsum spread: the salt washed out and the farmland is back to normal
block.semiconductor-lab.refrigerator.how: Add water buckets and ammonia water (not used up), then connect power. Ice comes out and the bucket returns.
